summary: SSRI antidepressant used for depression and several anxiety-related conditions (panic, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety). Effective, but more likely than many SSRIs to cause withdrawal symptoms if stopped abruptly and can be activating early on.
description: Paroxetine is an SSRI that can treat depression, panic, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety, and generalized anxiety. It’s usually taken once daily. Many people feel side effects first (nausea, sleep changes, sweating, sexual side effects), then benefits build over weeks. It carries the class boxed warning about suicidal thoughts in people under 25. Don’t stop suddenly—paroxetine is one of the SSRIs most likely to cause withdrawal symptoms.
patient_summary: Paroxetine can help depression and anxiety disorders, but it’s not a “take it and feel better today” med. Early side effects are common, benefits build over weeks, and stopping too fast can feel awful. If you’re under 25, your prescriber should watch closely for mood worsening or suicidal thoughts early in treatment and after dose changes.

primary.context: Used for unipolar depression. Expect early side effects first, then gradual improvement over 2 to 6 weeks.
A common SSRI option for GAD. Some people who are anxiety-sensitive do better starting low and going up slowly to avoid feeling overstimulated early on.
Used for panic disorder (with or without agoraphobia). Starting low is key because early activation can briefly feel like “more panic” before it gets better.
Often requires higher doses and longer trials than depression. A fair OCD trial is typically weeks at the maximum tolerated dose.
Used for PTSD. Benefits build gradually and may continue improving over 4 to 12+ weeks.
Can help social anxiety. Dose increases are usually slow, especially if early jitters or insomnia show up.
Paroxetine CR is used for PMDD. Some patients use continuous dosing; others use luteal-phase or symptom-onset strategies depending on symptom pattern.

off_label.context: Sometimes used as an alternative SSRI option for body dysmorphic disorder, often requiring higher doses and a longer time window to judge response.

therapeutic_response.display: Depression: some early effects in 1 to 2 weeks; anxiety disorders: early effects may appear within ~2 weeks with continued improvement through 4 to 6 weeks; OCD/PTSD may require longer trials

common_adverse_effects.notes: Usually worst early and often improves over 1 to 2 weeks. Taking with food can help.
Some people feel wired at night early on. If that’s you, morning dosing and slow titration can help.
The opposite pattern can happen too—sleepiness or ‘heavy’ fatigue. Give it time, and discuss timing adjustments with your prescriber.
Annoying but common. Hydration and breathable clothing help; persistent severe sweating is worth addressing.
This can be one of the biggest deal-breakers. It’s real, it’s common, and there are strategies (dose adjustments, switching, or add-on options) if it doesn’t improve.
Early activation can feel like your anxiety is worse. Starting low and titrating slowly can reduce this.

serious_risks.risk: Suicidal thoughts/behaviors (increased risk in people under 25, especially early in treatment or with dose changes)
Mania/hypomania activation (especially in bipolar spectrum illness or with risk factors)
Serotonin syndrome (more likely with other serotonergic drugs; can be life-threatening)
Hyponatremia/SIADH (confusion, headache, weakness; higher risk in older adults and with diuretics)
Abnormal bleeding (especially with NSAIDs, antiplatelets, anticoagulants)
Severe hypersensitivity reactions (including serious skin reactions)
Severe discontinuation syndrome if stopped abruptly (dizziness, shock-like sensations, agitation, insomnia, nausea, tremor)

safety.black_box_warning: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to paroxetine or any component (including severe reactions such as anaphylaxis, angioedema, Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN)
Concurrent use with, or within 14 days of, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), including linezolid and IV methylene blue
Concomitant use with thioridazine (QT prolongation risk)
Concomitant use with pimozide (QT prolongation risk)

precautions: Not approved for pediatric patients for psychiatric use (paroxetine specifically is not approved for pediatric patients)
Activation early in treatment: anxiety, agitation, insomnia, irritability, akathisia—these can look like “worse anxiety” at first
Mania/hypomania risk: antidepressants can trigger mood switching, especially in undiagnosed bipolar spectrum illness
Serotonin syndrome risk, especially when combined with other serotonergic medications
Bleeding risk: SSRIs can increase bleeding risk, especially with NSAIDs, antiplatelets, or anticoagulants
Hyponatremia/SIADH risk (more common in older adults or those on diuretics)
CNS effects: may impair alertness in some people; be cautious with driving until you know your response
QT concerns: cases of QT prolongation have been reported (causality not always clear); avoid contraindicated QT-risk combos like thioridazine and pimozide

interactions.interactant: MAOIs (including linezolid and IV methylene blue)
interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated due to serotonin syndrome risk.
interactions.action: Allow 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting paroxetine, and 14 days between stopping paroxetine and starting an MAOI.

interactions.interactant: Other serotonergic meds (other SSRIs/SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, linezolid, lithium, St. John’s wort, certain migraine and pain meds)
interactions.action: Avoid high-risk combinations when possible. If used, monitor closely for agitation, confusion, tremor, muscle rigidity, fever, sweating, diarrhea, rapid heart rate.

interactions.mechanism: Higher bleeding risk (easy bruising, nosebleeds, GI bleeding).
interactions.action: Use caution and monitor. Consider GI protection if clinically appropriate and discuss risks with the prescriber.

interactions.action: Medication review is essential. Dose adjustments or alternative meds may be needed.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Suicidality and clinical worsening: especially in the first 1 to 2 months, and during any dose increases or decreases; monitor closely in patients under 25
Activation symptoms: anxiety, agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia—especially early in treatment
Mania/hypomania: screen for bipolar history and monitor for mood switching (decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, risky behavior)
Serotonin syndrome: especially with serotonergic combinations; watch for agitation, tremor, rigidity, fever, confusion, diarrhea, autonomic instability
Hyponatremia/SIADH: check sodium in at-risk populations (older adults, diuretics, low baseline sodium, low body weight, prior hyponatremia)
Bleeding risk: bruising, nosebleeds, GI bleeding—especially with NSAIDs/antiplatelets/anticoagulants
Sexual function: libido, arousal, orgasm; track because it often impacts adherence
Weight and appetite changes over time
Renal and hepatic function tests: baseline and as clinically indicated, especially in impairment
Withdrawal/discontinuation symptoms: dizziness, shock-like sensations, insomnia, irritability, nausea—especially if doses are missed or tapering is too fast

special_populations.pregnancy: Paroxetine crosses the placenta. Some studies suggest a less than 2-fold increased risk of certain congenital heart malformations with first-trimester exposure, though results vary. Late-pregnancy SSRI exposure can be associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome (usually resolves within ~2 weeks) and a rare risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Treatment decisions should be shared decision-making: untreated depression/anxiety also carries pregnancy risks. If initiating an SSRI in a treatment-naive pregnant patient, an SSRI other than paroxetine is often preferred; patients stable and doing well may sometimes continue paroxetine if benefits outweigh risks and no contraindications exist. Brisdelle (for vasomotor symptoms) is contraindicated in pregnancy.
special_populations.lactation: Paroxetine is present in breast milk, typically with a low relative infant dose (commonly reported in the ~0.5% to 3% range). Breastfeeding is often considered acceptable, but infants should be monitored for irritability, sleep changes, feeding issues, lethargy, and weight gain. The manufacturer recommends weighing the importance of maternal treatment against potential infant risk.
special_populations.pediatric: Paroxetine is not approved for pediatric patients. Antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies; close monitoring is required. If used in rare refractory cases under specialist care, start low and titrate slowly with close monitoring for activation and suicidality.
special_populations.geriatric: Often avoided in adults ≥65 because paroxetine has stronger anticholinergic properties than many SSRIs and may increase sedation and orthostatic hypotension, contributing to falls. If used despite risks, start low and titrate cautiously; monitor sodium and falls risk closely.
special_populations.renal_impairment: CrCl >60 mL/min: no adjustment typically needed. With CrCl 30 to 60 mL/min, exposure may increase; consider reducing the initial dose by ~25% to 50% and titrate based on response/tolerability. With CrCl <30 mL/min, start lower (IR 5 to 10 mg/day or ER 12.5 mg/day) and do not exceed reduced maximums (often capped around 40 mg/day IR or 50 mg/day ER, or the indication-specific max—whichever is lower).
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Use caution in hepatic impairment because clearance can be decreased and exposure increased. For preexisting cirrhosis, use the lowest recommended indication-specific dose and titrate carefully; some severe impairment scenarios use lower maximums (often capped around 40 mg/day IR or 50 mg/day ER, or the indication-specific max—whichever is lower).

pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Immediate-release tablets/suspension: ~5 to 8 hours; controlled-release tablets: ~6 to 10 hours; capsules: median ~6 hours
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Approximately 15 to 21 hours (varies by formulation; can be prolonged in certain situations, including overdose)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism; CYP2D6 plays a major role; nonlinear pharmacokinetics can occur due to saturation
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (~64%, ~2% unchanged) and feces (~36%, mostly via bile)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Peak concentration may increase, but overall bioavailability is not significantly altered

dosing.titration: Paroxetine comes in immediate-release (IR) and extended-release (ER/CR). Both are taken once daily, but they are not interchangeable mg-for-mg. Many clinicians start lower in anxiety-sensitive patients to reduce early activation (jittery anxiety, insomnia).

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Paroxetine is one of the SSRIs most likely to cause discontinuation symptoms if stopped abruptly. If you’ve taken it for 4+ weeks, plan a taper—don’t improvise a sudden stop.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Paroxetine is an SSRI used for depression and several anxiety-spectrum conditions. It’s taken once daily, and it works by gradually shifting serotonin signaling over time (weeks, not hours). It can be a solid option, but it’s also known for stronger withdrawal symptoms if stopped too fast compared with many other SSRIs.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Persistent low mood, loss of interest, low energy, impaired concentration
{link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)}: Chronic worry, tension, and physical anxiety symptoms
{link:condition:panic-disorder:Panic Disorder}: Recurrent panic attacks and fear of future attacks
{link:condition:obsessive-compulsive-disorder:Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)}: Intrusive thoughts and compulsive behaviors
{link:condition:posttraumatic-stress-disorder:Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)}: Trauma-related symptoms, hyperarousal, re-experiencing, avoidance
{link:condition:social-anxiety-disorder:Social Anxiety Disorder}: Intense fear of social situations and judgment
{link:condition:premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder:Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)}: Severe cyclical mood symptoms tied to the menstrual cycle

sections.heading: What People Feel

items.category: Week 1–2: “My body noticed it before my mood did”
quotes: I felt kind of queasy and restless before I felt any relief.
Sleep got weird at first—either wired at night or sleepy all day.
It felt like my anxiety was louder for a few days, then it started to level out.
items.note: Early activation (jittery, insomnia, increased anxiety) can happen, especially if you start too high or you’re sensitive.

quotes: The panic stopped escalating as fast. I could interrupt it.
My baseline felt calmer—less bracing-for-impact all day.
I didn’t feel ‘happy,’ but I felt more stable and functional.

items.category: OCD/PTSD timelines: “It’s slower than I want”
quotes: OCD didn’t budge at first. Then small wins started stacking.
The intrusive stuff got less sticky over time.
PTSD symptoms improved gradually—sleep and reactivity shifted first.
items.note: OCD and some PTSD presentations may need longer trials and sometimes higher doses to really judge response.

items.category: Sexual side effects: “My brain is willing, my body is not”
quotes: Libido dipped and orgasms were harder—annoying but real.
It helped my anxiety, but sex felt kind of muted.
items.note: Sexual dysfunction is a common SSRI issue and can be dose-related.

items.category: Stopping too fast: “I learned the hard way”
quotes: Missed a couple doses and felt electric zaps and dizziness.
I got irritable, nauseated, and couldn’t sleep—like my nervous system was mad.
Tapering slowly was the difference between miserable and manageable.
items.note: Paroxetine is one of the SSRIs most associated with discontinuation symptoms—slow tapering matters.

sections.intro: Paroxetine is one of those meds where the timeline matters: side effects often show up first, and benefits build later. Here’s how people commonly describe it:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Paroxetine isn’t a fast-acting “take it and feel calm in an hour” medication. Think in weeks. Side effects may show up early; benefits build with steady daily dosing.
key_points: Days 1–7: Side effects are more likely than benefits (nausea, sleep changes, jittery activation, sweating)
Week 1–2: Some people notice early shifts (less crying, slightly better sleep, slightly less panic reactivity)
Weeks 4–6: More dependable improvement window for depression and many anxiety disorders
OCD/PTSD: May need a longer runway (often 8–12+ weeks to judge a true response, depending on symptoms and dose)
Half-life ~15–21 hours: Missing doses can trigger withdrawal symptoms in some people, sometimes within days

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Paroxetine can be effective for depression and multiple anxiety-spectrum conditions, but it generally takes consistent daily dosing for weeks to see meaningful change. If you’re treating OCD or certain PTSD patterns, the trial may need to be longer (and sometimes at higher doses) before calling it a success or failure.
sections.clinical_details: For depression, early effects may appear within 1 to 2 weeks with continued improvement through 4 to 6 weeks. For anxiety disorders (GAD, panic, OCD, PTSD), initial effects may be observed within ~2 weeks with continued improvements through 4 to 6 weeks; OCD and PTSD may require longer trials to assess response.

patient_counseling: If you’re under 25, expect closer monitoring early on and after dose changes. If suicidal thoughts increase, reach out immediately.
If you feel newly agitated, restless, unable to sit still (akathisia), or your insomnia spikes—tell your prescriber. That can be a treatable side effect, not a personal failure.
Do not combine with MAOIs. Also avoid contraindicated meds like thioridazine and pimozide.
Don’t stop suddenly. Paroxetine withdrawal can be intense—plan a taper.
If you develop symptoms like confusion, fever, muscle rigidity, tremor, severe agitation, or rapid heart rate—get urgent care for possible serotonin syndrome.
If you bruise easily, get nosebleeds, or have GI bleeding symptoms—tell your clinician, especially if you take NSAIDs or blood thinners.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common themes: GI upset (especially nausea), sleep changes (insomnia or sleepiness), sweating, sexual dysfunction, and activation early on. Paroxetine also has relatively stronger anticholinergic-style effects compared with many SSRIs, and it’s well-known for discontinuation symptoms if stopped quickly.

Withdrawal symptoms if you miss doses or stop abruptly (dizziness, “brain zaps,” irritability, insomnia)

sections.intro: Paroxetine has two big interaction themes: (1) serotonin interactions (serotonin syndrome risk) and (2) CYP2D6 effects (it’s a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor).

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Paroxetine is one of the SSRIs most likely to cause discontinuation symptoms if stopped abruptly. If you’ve taken it for 4+ weeks, plan a taper—don’t improvise a sudden stop.
key_points: Common withdrawal symptoms: dizziness, chills, vertigo, ‘brain zaps’/shock-like sensations, nausea, tremor, diarrhea, insomnia, irritability, anxiety, confusion
Typical onset: 1 to 10 days after abrupt stop or too-fast taper (sometimes sooner if doses are missed)
If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: taper gradually over ~3 to 4 weeks as a common starting approach; slower tapers may be needed
If brief treatment (2 to 3 weeks): some people taper over 1 to 2 weeks; <2 weeks often doesn’t require a taper
Reasons to go slower (≥4 weeks or longer): prior withdrawal history, higher doses, longer duration, high sensitivity
If withdrawal becomes intolerable: return to the prior dose and taper more gradually
Long-term treatment (>6 months): some patients may benefit from tapering over >3 months

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Paroxetine comes in immediate-release (IR) and extended-release (ER/CR). Both are taken once daily, but they are not interchangeable mg-for-mg. Many clinicians start lower in anxiety-sensitive patients to reduce early activation (jittery anxiety, insomnia).

adult.mdd_ir_titration: Increase by 10 to 20 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.mdd_er_titration: Increase by 12.5 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.gad_ir_titration: Increase by 10 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.panic_ir_initial: 10 mg PO once daily for 3 to 7 days
adult.panic_ir_titration: Increase by 10 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.panic_er_titration: Increase by 12.5 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.ocd_ir_titration: Increase by 10 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.ocd_ir_max: 60 mg/day (some specialists use higher doses when tolerated, with careful risk/benefit)
adult.ptsd_ir_titration: Increase by 10 to 20 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.social_anxiety_ir_titration: After 4 to 6 weeks at the initial dose, increase by 10 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week as needed based on response and tolerability
adult.social_anxiety_er_titration: After 4 to 6 weeks at the initial dose, increase by 12.5 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week as needed based on response and tolerability
adult.social_anxiety_er_max: 37.5 mg/day (some specialists use higher equivalent doses when needed, with careful risk/benefit)
adult.pmdd_er_continuous_initial: 12.5 mg PO once daily (continuous daily dosing)
adult.pmdd_er_continuous_titration: Increase to 25 mg once daily over the first month; in a subsequent cycle may increase further based on response
adult.pmdd_ir_continuous_offlabel_initial: 10 mg PO once daily (continuous daily dosing)
adult.pmdd_ir_continuous_offlabel_titration: Increase to 20 mg once daily over the first month; in a subsequent cycle may increase further based on response
adult.pmdd_ir_luteal_offlabel_initial: 10 mg PO once daily during the luteal phase only (start ~14 days before anticipated menses and continue to onset of menses)
adult.pmdd_ir_luteal_offlabel_titration: Increase to 20 mg once daily during luteal phase over the first month; in a subsequent cycle may increase further based on response
adult.pmdd_er_luteal_initial: 12.5 mg PO once daily during the luteal phase only (start ~14 days before anticipated menses and continue to onset of menses)
adult.pmdd_er_luteal_titration: Increase to 25 mg once daily during luteal phase over the first month; in a subsequent cycle may increase further based on response
adult.pmdd_er_luteal_max: 37.5 mg/day during luteal phase (based on equivalent IR dose)
adult.pmdd_ir_symptom_onset_offlabel: 10 mg PO once daily from symptom onset until a few days after start of menses; may increase based on response up to 20 mg/day, and in later cycles up to 30 mg/day if needed
adult.bdd_ir_offlabel_titration: Increase by 20 mg/day every 2 to 3 weeks based on response and tolerability
adult.bdd_ir_offlabel_max: 100 mg/day (specialist-level dosing when tolerated, if needed for optimal response)
adult.sensitive_patient_low_start: Some experts start lower (IR 5 to 10 mg once daily or ER 12.5 mg once daily) and titrate gradually, especially in anxiety-sensitive patients who get overstimulated early (anxiety, insomnia).
adult.dosing_conversion_note: IR and ER are not interchangeable mg-for-mg; a commonly cited conversion is IR 10 mg ≈ ER 12.5 mg.

sections.simple_explanation: Paroxetine works gradually. Starting low and increasing slowly can reduce early activation. IR and ER both use once-daily dosing, but ER is not the same dose-for-dose as IR. The goal is the lowest effective dose that improves symptoms without causing side effects you can’t tolerate.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Paroxetine requires extra thought in pregnancy planning, older adults, and anyone at higher risk of hyponatremia or bleeding. It also carries the antidepressant class warning about suicidality in younger people.

Brisdelle (for vasomotor symptoms) is contraindicated in pregnancy.

The manufacturer recommends weighing the importance of maternal treatment against potential infant risk.

If used in rare refractory cases under specialist care, start low and titrate slowly with close monitoring for activation and suicidality.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Paroxetine comes in immediate-release and controlled-release (CR) forms. They are both once-daily, but not interchangeable milligram-for-milligram. There’s also a low-dose capsule marketed for menopausal vasomotor symptoms (not a psychiatric dose).
items: Immediate-release tablets: 10 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg, 40 mg
Oral suspension: 10 mg/5 mL
Controlled-release (CR) tablets: 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 37.5 mg (swallow whole; do not crush/chew)
Capsule (paroxetine mesylate) 7.5 mg: marketed for vasomotor symptoms of menopause (Brisdelle); not a psychiatric-dose product

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Paroxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). In simple terms, it increases serotonin signaling by blocking serotonin reuptake at synapses. Over time, this shifts stress, mood, and fear-circuit activity in a way that can reduce depression and anxiety symptoms.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Paroxetine can be effective for depression and multiple anxiety-spectrum conditions, but it’s not always the first SSRI clinicians reach for. Compared with many SSRIs, paroxetine is more likely to cause withdrawal symptoms if stopped abruptly and has relatively stronger anticholinergic-style side effects (dry mouth, constipation, sedation, orthostasis), which matters a lot in older adults. It can still be a good fit when it works well for someone, when prior SSRI trials failed, or when the symptom cluster responds specifically to it—just with a strong plan for monitoring early activation and for tapering when it’s time to stop.

faqs.a: Paroxetine is an SSRI used for major depression and several anxiety-spectrum conditions, including generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, and PMDD (often with the controlled-release form). It’s taken once daily and works gradually over weeks.

faqs.q: How long does paroxetine take to work?
faqs.a: Most people don’t feel full benefits in the first few days. Early changes can show up in 1 to 2 weeks, with more reliable improvement around weeks 4 to 6 for depression and many anxiety disorders. OCD and some PTSD cases may take longer to judge, sometimes 8 to 12+ weeks depending on symptoms and dose.

faqs.q: Why do some people feel more anxious at the start?
faqs.a: SSRIs can be activating early on—jittery energy, insomnia, agitation, or a temporary spike in anxiety. Starting at a lower dose and increasing slowly can reduce this. If you feel intensely restless, panicky, or unable to sit still (akathisia), tell your prescriber right away.

faqs.q: Does paroxetine cause sexual side effects?
faqs.a: It can. Like other SSRIs, paroxetine is commonly linked to reduced libido, delayed orgasm, ejaculatory delay, or erectile dysfunction. If it happens and doesn’t improve, there are options—dose adjustments, switching medications, or add-on strategies—so bring it up rather than suffering quietly.

No—don’t stop abruptly unless a clinician specifically tells you to for a safety reason. Paroxetine is one of the SSRIs most likely to cause discontinuation symptoms (dizziness, nausea, irritability, insomnia, “brain zaps”). A gradual taper is the usual plan.

faqs.q: What are ‘brain zaps’ and why do they happen?
faqs.a: People describe ‘brain zaps’ as brief shock-like sensations, often with dizziness or a weird ‘electric’ feeling. They can happen when paroxetine is stopped too fast or doses are missed. The fix is usually a slower taper (or temporarily going back to the prior dose and tapering more gradually).

faqs.q: Is there a boxed warning about suicide risk?
faqs.a: Yes. Antidepressants can increase suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teens, and young adults (under 25) in short-term studies, especially early in treatment and after dose changes. That doesn’t mean everyone gets worse—but it does mean monitoring is essential.

faqs.q: What medications should never be combined with paroxetine?
faqs.a: MAOIs (and you must separate them by a 14-day washout), plus thioridazine and pimozide due to serious heart rhythm risk. Also be careful with other serotonergic meds because of serotonin syndrome risk, and with blood thinners/NSAIDs because of bleeding risk.

faqs.q: Is paroxetine safe in older adults?
faqs.a: Often it’s avoided in adults 65+ because paroxetine has stronger anticholinergic properties than many SSRIs and can contribute to sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and falls. If it’s used, clinicians usually start low, go slow, and monitor closely (including sodium in at-risk patients).

faqs.q: What’s the difference between Paxil and Paxil CR?
faqs.a: They’re both paroxetine, but Paxil is immediate-release (IR) and Paxil CR is controlled-release (CR). Both are once daily, but they are not interchangeable dose-for-dose. CR is designed to release more gradually, and many dosing schedules use 12.5 mg step increases.

faqs.q: Is Brisdelle the same thing as Paxil?
faqs.a: Brisdelle is a low-dose paroxetine (7.5 mg capsule) marketed for menopausal hot flashes, not psychiatric conditions. If someone needs paroxetine for depression or anxiety, Brisdelle is not a psychiatric-dose product.
